A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViPO work and have readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after the references; v3 retains the main paper and adds supplementary Sections A–C. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original Flux and Wan2.1 experiments, including quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–2, ablations in Tables 3–4, and qualitative redness-reward experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and additionally reports computational overhead, detailed VBench results and further qualitative analyses in the supplement.

M1.justification: The PSM, spatial advantage assignment and ViPO objective in Sections 3.2–3.3 remain unchanged. Appendix A specifies computations for the already evaluated DINOv2, SAM and ResNet variants; it does not establish a change to the implemented method.

E1.justification: Both versions use HPD image prompts, VidProM video prompts, VBench evaluation and the redness-reward setting. Additional qualitative examples and VBench breakdowns retain this coverage without introducing a distinct dataset, domain or task.

E2.justification: DanceGRPO and the untuned Flux/Wan2.1 models remain the comparison methods, with the same PSM backbone variants. The supplement reuses these comparators. Figure 10 explicitly labels the Flux reference for redness optimization; Figure 5 already displayed the shared starting outputs.

E3.justification: Table 5 adds an efficiency evaluation using training-step time, per-sample PSM latency and peak memory. Existing splits, resolutions, sampling steps and quality-evaluation settings remain unchanged. Appendix C discloses additional settings for the retained experiments without stating that those settings were changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds resource-overhead analysis in Table 5 and mechanism diagnostics through backbone-specific allocation maps and individual PCA components in Figure 8. Figures 9–10 further examine backbone-dependent outputs and semantic preservation under redness optimization. These substantially extend efficiency and mechanism analyses, while the quantitative ablations in Tables 3–4 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seed lists, confidence intervals or significance tests. Appendix C's shared initialization noise within each sample group describes sampling control rather than statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their scores, but v3 adds substantial efficiency and detailed performance evidence. Table 5 reports image training-time overhead of 1.0–1.8% and video overhead of 4.8%. Table 6 adds nine VBench dimensions: Dynamic Degree is 63.89 for ViPO, 45.83 for DanceGRPO and 52.77 for Wan2.1; ViPO nevertheless trails Wan2.1 on Color, Appearance Style and Scene. Additional figures report further qualitative outputs and allocation maps.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds explicit mathematical definitions for inverted min-max normalization and CNN channel aggregation using softmax weights derived from global average pooling. Other appendix equations restate the existing PCA and variance-weighted construction. The original equations and reasoning remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about structured visual advantages, annotation-free perceptual allocation, improved preference alignment and lightweight compatibility with GRPO. The supplement adds support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds interpretations of DINOv2's semantic emphasis, ResNet's texture responses and SAM's boundary emphasis, including cases where SAM weights backgrounds more strongly than foregrounds. Appendix B additionally suggests that semantic alignment improves indirectly despite excluding text alignment from the training reward.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C substantially expand reproducibility information previously deferred to unavailable supplementary material in v1. Additions include precise map computations, ResNet-50 layer4 extraction, learning rates, SDE noise parameters, a 0.6 gradient-timestep fraction, shared group initialization, a 1e-4 clipping range and video generation/reward-processing frame rates. These are newly documented details, without evidence of changed training settings.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning remain the same. Reference 21 changes from preprint metadata to its journal publication, and the supplement reuses existing backbone citations; neither constitutes a new related-work contribution.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely unchanged. v3 corrects the author spelling Haibing to Haibin, several typographical errors and a duplicated phrase, and organizes the supplementary explanations into Sections A–C. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing argument.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–6 and Figures 6–10, providing extensive image/video comparison grids, allocation-map and PCA visualizations, backbone comparisons and additional redness examples. These substantially expand the visual presentation while preserving the main tables and figures; Figure 1 also receives a spelling correction.

improvement.justification: v1 defers essential PSM computations and training settings to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. v3 supplies those details in Appendices A and C, substantially improving reproducibility. Measured overhead and allocation-map diagnostics also provide concrete support for previously asserted efficiency and mechanism claims, while detailed VBench scores expose performance boundaries. The headline experiments remain unchanged and statistical uncertainty is still unreported, but the documentation and supporting-evidence gains are substantial.
